title: Put a Little Drama in Your Travel
description: The lesson that runs in two directions at once, and has no grammar of its own: reading squeezes prose into notes, writing opens notes back into prose. On one side, a festival programme read as the four questions it answers - which play, which troupe, in what venue, on which dates - with the traps that cost marks (a venue is the exact spot and not the town, a dash between two dates opens a run of every evening and not two performances, the playwright wrote the words while the troupe performs them tonight), the words of the season (venue, troupe, playwright, dramatist, the Bard, choreography, sightseeing, to head for, on the calendar, a cybertrip, to stage a play and a stage to act on), and the byline, the agency and the date above a travel article, which prove that a festival exists without ever giving this year's days. In the middle, the dictionary opened properly in four steps - the base form first, then the noun half or the verb half according to the word's job in your sentence, then the numbered senses inside that half, and the fixed expressions filed last behind their own label - plus what an entry gives beyond meanings: the pronunciation, the American spelling, and the grammar hidden in its little example. On the other side, a biography written from a box of bare notes: giving each note back its subject, its verb in the past and its small words, keeping the years in line, opening on who the person was rather than on a date, and above all adding nothing the notes do not carry - a fact worked out from two dates is allowed, a reason or a judgement nobody wrote down is not - with the eight linkers of the book (and, after, but, next, then, in the end, eventually, some time later) weighed for what each one actually claims
